chapterName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Origins (509-450 BCE)

questions.question: Where did the plebs secede to in 449 BC?
options: The Aventine Hill, then the Sacred Mount
questions.explanation: In the second secession the plebs went to the Aventine Hill and then the Sacred Mount. The decemvirs were forced out as a result.
questions.sourceQuote: In 449 BC the plebs seceded again, to the Aventine Hill and then the Sacred Mount.

questions.question: According to tradition, what fable did Agrippa Menenius Lanatus tell the seceding plebeians?
options: The geese that saved the Capitol
The wolf who nursed two abandoned twins
The ant who stored grain for winter
The limbs of a body that refused to feed the belly
questions.explanation: He told of limbs that refused to feed the belly, only to starve themselves. A city, he argued, likewise needed patricians and plebeians working together.
questions.sourceQuote: He told a fable about the limbs of a body that refused to feed the belly, only to starve themselves.

questions.question: After the kings were gone, who served as Rome's chief magistrates?
options: Ten tribunes elected every five years
A single dictator elected for life
Two consuls elected for one year at a time
Three kings sharing power for a decade
questions.explanation: Two consuls, elected for one-year terms, ran the state together with the Senate, a council of leading men. Every one of these positions belonged to the patricians.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead of a monarch, two consuls, chief magistrates elected for one year at a time, ran the state alongside the Senate, a council of leading men.

questions.question: What was the tribunes' strongest weapon?
questions.explanation: The veto let tribunes block the actions of magistrates. This power rested on tribunes being sacrosanct.
questions.sourceQuote: The tribunes' strongest weapon was the veto, the power to block the actions of magistrates.

questions.question: Which tribune declared in 462 BC that rule by consuls had become more oppressive than the monarchy?
questions.explanation: Gaius Terentilius Arsa argued that the consuls' powers needed clear limits. His campaign eventually led to the writing down of Roman law.
questions.sourceQuote: In 462 BC the tribune Gaius Terentilius Arsa declared that rule by consuls had become even more oppressive than the monarchy it replaced.

questions.question: Which decemvir is at the centre of the famous story of Verginia?
questions.explanation: Appius Claudius Crassus tried to seize Verginia, daughter of a respected centurion. The scandal sparked riots that spread to the army.
questions.sourceQuote: The most famous story concerns the decemvir Appius Claudius Crassus.

questions.question: Which tribune carried the Lex Publilia of 471 BC?
questions.explanation: The tribune Volero Publilius carried the reform in 471 BC. It made the plebs politically independent by breaking patrician influence over their votes.
questions.sourceQuote: In 471 BC a tribune named Volero Publilius carried a reform known as the Lex Publilia.

questions.question: In the early Republic, which group held every position of power?
questions.explanation: The patricians were a small hereditary aristocracy who monopolised the consulship and the Senate. Everyone else was a plebeian, and plebeians made up the great majority of citizens.
questions.sourceQuote: Every one of these positions belonged to the patricians, a small hereditary aristocracy.

questions.question: What does the Latin word 'decemviri' mean?
questions.explanation: The decemviri were a commission of 'ten men' appointed to govern for a year and write down Roman law. There was no appeal against their decisions.
questions.sourceQuote: In their place a commission called the decemviri, Latin for 'ten men', would govern for a year and write down Roman law, with no appeal against their decisions.

questions.question: Which modern scholar argues that there was no Conflict of the Orders at all?
questions.explanation: Richard E. Mitchell is among the scholars who argue there was no conflict at all. In this view, later Romans projected their own class struggles onto the distant past.
questions.sourceQuote: Some scholars, such as Richard E. Mitchell, argue there was no conflict at all.
